title: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
summary: Turn free text into typed spans: BIO and BIOES tag sets, entity-level micro F1 with exact match, CRF transitions and Viterbi by hand, BERT taggers with subword alignment, and weak supervision on logs.
outcomes: Explain why NER is per-token labelling plus a span decoder, and why a tag set needs a B marker at all.
Compute entity-level micro precision, recall and F1 with exact span match, and say why one boundary error costs two.
Run Viterbi by hand on a 3 token, 3 label table and explain what a CRF transition matrix adds over independent softmaxes.
Align word-level labels to WordPiece tokens for a BERT tagger and evaluate back at the word level.
Pick between gazetteers, weak supervision and fine-tuning when labels are scarce in a new domain such as logs.

lessons.title: The task: pull typed spans out of running text

blocks.md:
Named entity recognition (NER) takes a piece of text and returns the typed spans inside it. Given the sentence `U.N. staff met Ekeus in Rome .` a tagger should return three entities: `U.N.` as an organisation, `Ekeus` as a person, `Rome` as a location.

This matters whenever the next step in a pipeline needs fields rather than prose. A log line such as `web-04 ERROR authd code=E503 db-7 timed out` carries a host, a component and an error code, and you cannot group, join or alert on any of them until something has marked where each one starts and ends.

The shared task that defined the modern setup is CoNLL-2003. Its English data is Reuters newswire with four entity types: person (PER), location (LOC), organisation (ORG) and a catch-all miscellaneous class (MISC) for things like `Italian` or `1000 Lakes Rally`.

The obvious first attempt is a dictionary. Collect every entity string you saw in training, then mark those strings wherever they appear again.

The CoNLL-2003 organisers ran exactly this as the official baseline: tag only phrases that had a single unambiguous class in the training data, preferring the longest match. On the English test set it scored precision 71.91 percent, recall 50.90 percent, F1 59.61 percent.

Look at the shape of that failure. Precision is mediocre and recall is terrible: the unambiguous phrases memorised from training match only about half of the entities in the test set. The training and development sets are news from August 1996 while the test set is news from December 1996, so the names are mostly different people, companies and places. Memorising names cannot work, because names are an open class. The model has to learn the *context* that signals an entity.

blocks.title: F1 on the CoNLL-2003 English test set, 2003 to 2019

scenes.caption: The official baseline memorises unambiguous training phrases: 59.61 F1, with recall only 50.90 percent because test names are new.
The best of the sixteen 2003 entries, a classifier combination, reached 88.76 F1 using hand-built features and gazetteers, which are lists of known entity names.
A BiLSTM-CRF with pretrained embeddings reached 90.94 and a fine-tuned BERT-large 92.8 on the same test set. All four numbers are entity-level F1.

blocks.md:
So how do you learn context? The trick that made NER tractable is to stop predicting spans directly and predict one label per token instead. That turns an unbounded structured output (any set of non-overlapping intervals with types) into a sequence of ordinary classification decisions, one per token, which any classifier, recurrent net or transformer can produce.

Spans come back out in a second step: a small deterministic decoder scans the label sequence and groups neighbouring tokens into entities.

Entities are sparse, which is why this is hard. The CoNLL-2003 English training set has 14,987 sentences and 203,621 tokens holding 23,499 entities (7,140 LOC, 6,321 ORG, 6,600 PER, 3,438 MISC): about 1.57 entities per sentence, one entity per 8.7 tokens. Most tokens are outside everything.

blocks.title: Per-token labels, then a span decoder

scenes.caption: The input is a tokenised sentence. Nothing yet says where entities begin or end.
The model emits one label per token. B-X opens an entity of type X, I-X continues one, O means outside any entity.
The decoder walks the labels left to right and emits three single-token spans. Every entity here is one token long, which is the common case in newswire.

blocks.md: An NER system is three pieces that must agree with each other: a **tag set** that can represent any set of non-overlapping spans, a **model** that scores tag sequences, and a **decoder** that turns tags back into spans. Most NER bugs live in the seams between them, not in the model.

blocks.prompt: Suppose you label each token with just the type or nothing: LOC, ORG, PER, MISC, O. Now tag the sentence `New York Paris staff left .` where `New York` is one location and `Paris` is another. What does the decoder see?
blocks.reveal:
It sees `LOC LOC LOC O O O` and cannot tell whether that is one three-token location, two locations, or three. The type-only tag set loses the entity boundaries, so the decoder has to guess, and any guess is wrong on some sentence.

This is precisely why the tag set carries a boundary marker. The next lesson builds the fix.

blocks.question: Why did the memorisation baseline reach precision 71.91 percent but recall only 50.90 percent on the CoNLL-2003 English test set?
options: Entity names are rare in newswire, so there was little to memorise
Names are an open class and the test set is from a different month, so a dictionary of training phrases matches only about half of its entities
The baseline used the wrong tag set and so could not represent multi-token spans
Precision and recall are measured on different entity types
blocks.explain: Train and dev are August 1996 Reuters news, test is December 1996. New stories mean new names, and a dictionary cannot find a name it never saw. When it does fire it is often right, which is why precision is much higher than recall.

blocks.question: What does the reduction to per-token labelling buy you?
options: It removes the need for a decoder, since the labels are already the spans
It lets the model predict overlapping entities
It guarantees the predicted spans are always valid
It turns an unbounded structured output into one fixed-size classification per position, which any classifier can emit
blocks.explain: One label per token is a fixed-size decision per position, which any classifier can emit. You still need a decoder, the output can still be an invalid tag sequence, and a single chain of labels cannot represent overlapping spans at all.

lessons.title: BIO, IOB1 and BIOES: tag sets that make spans decodable

blocks.md:
The fix for the ambiguity you just saw comes from text chunking, not from NER. Ramshaw and Marcus introduced the chunk tag set {I, O, B} in 1995, where (quoting them) "words marked I are inside some baseNP, those marked O are outside, and the B tag is used to mark the left most item of a baseNP which immediately follows another baseNP".

That is the scheme the CoNLL-2003 data files actually use, now usually called **IOB1**: entity tokens get I-X by default, and B-X appears only to split two adjacent entities of the same type. It is economical, because B is rare in the data.

Almost all modern code converts the data to **IOB2** (commonly just called BIO) first: every entity starts with B-X and continues with I-X, with no exceptions. The decoder then needs no lookahead and no special cases, and every tag is locally interpretable.

blocks.title: Three tag sets on two adjacent locations

scenes.caption: Gold truth: New York is one location and Paris is another. A type-only tag set collapses them into one run of LOC labels and the boundary is lost.
IOB1, used by the CoNLL data files: I-LOC by default, and B-LOC only because a second location starts right after the first.
IOB2 marks every entity start with B. The tags are now locally readable: B always opens, I always continues the entity on its left.
BIOES adds E for the last token of a multi-token entity and S for a single-token entity, so the end of a span is predicted explicitly rather than inferred from the next tag.

blocks.md:
BIOES (also written BILOU, with L for last and U for unit) costs you labels. With $n$ entity types, BIO needs $2n + 1$ labels and BIOES needs $4n + 1$: for the four CoNLL types that is 9 labels versus 17.

What you get back is a harder but more informative learning problem. The model must now commit to where a span ends, instead of leaving the end implicit in the following tag. Ratinov and Roth measured the difference with the same averaged-perceptron system on CoNLL-2003 English test: 89.15 F1 with BIO, 90.57 F1 with BILOU. They concluded that the encoding choice has a large effect on performance and used BILOU throughout their paper.

blocks.caption: Label-set sizes for the four CoNLL-2003 entity types. Every extra label is another column in the output layer and another row and column in the label-to-label transition matrix of lesson 4.

blocks.title: The span decoder, including the invalid I-after-O case

scenes.caption: The input is a predicted tag sequence, not gold data, so it may be anything the model emitted.
B-LOC opens a span whose start and end are both 0.
I-LOC matches the open span's type, so the end moves to 1. This is the only place a span grows.
O closes the open span and flushes it to the output list.
I-PER with nothing open is invalid under IOB2. The conlleval convention is to treat it as a span start anyway, which is what seqeval's default mode does.
Two spans come out. The second one exists only because of a repair rule inside the decoder, which is a good reason to stop the model emitting such sequences in the first place.

blocks.md: The repair rule is not cosmetic: it changes your score. [seqeval](https://github.com/chakki-works/seqeval) documents that for gold `B-NP I-NP O` and prediction `I-NP I-NP O`, its default mode (which mimics the conlleval Perl script) gives precision, recall and F1 of 1.00, while `mode='strict'` with `scheme=IOB2` gives 0.00. Same predictions, two different papers' worth of difference. Always say which mode you used.

blocks.question: In the CoNLL-2003 data files, when does a B-ORG tag appear?
options: Only when an organisation starts immediately after another organisation ends
At the start of every organisation entity
On every token of a multi-token organisation except the first
Only on single-token organisations
blocks.explain: The files use IOB1, the Ramshaw and Marcus scheme: entity tokens are I-ORG by default, and B-ORG marks only the leftmost token of an organisation that immediately follows another organisation. The option saying every organisation entity starts with B-ORG describes IOB2, which is what most modern pipelines convert the files to.

blocks.question: You switch a tagger from BIO to BIOES for 4 entity types and leave everything else alone. What definitely changes?
options: The number of entities in the gold data
The exact-match metric, because BIOES scores span ends separately
The output layer grows from 9 to 17 classes, and the model must now predict span ends explicitly
Nothing, since BIOES and BIO encode the same spans
blocks.explain: The two schemes encode the same spans, so the gold entities and the metric are unchanged. What changes is the learning problem: 17 classes instead of 9, with the end of each span becoming an explicit prediction. Ratinov and Roth measured that as 89.15 against 90.57 F1.

lessons.title: The metric: entity-level micro F1 with exact span match

blocks.md:
NER is scored on entities, not on tokens. The CoNLL-2003 rule is blunt: "A named entity is correct only if it is an exact match of the corresponding entity in the data file." Same start token, same end token, same type. There is no partial credit.

So you compare two sets of typed spans per sentence. A predicted span that is in the gold set is a true positive (TP), a predicted span that is not is a false positive (FP), and a gold span nobody predicted is a false negative (FN). Sum TP, FP and FN over the whole corpus first and divide once: that is the **micro** average, and it is what every CoNLL number in this course is.

blocks.caption: The CoNLL-2003 paper writes the general form with a beta weight and then sets beta to 1, which is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.

blocks.title: One sentence, two gold entities, three predicted ones

scenes.caption: Gold has two entities: LOC over tokens 1 to 2 and PER over tokens 5 to 6.
The model gets every type right and still breaks both entities: B-LOC twice splits San Jose in two, and the missing I-PER cuts Mary Smith short.
Exact match means the three predicted spans LOC(1,1), LOC(2,2), PER(5,5) are all wrong: 3 false positives, and both gold spans are missed, so 2 false negatives. Zero true positives on this sentence.

blocks.md:
Score a tiny three-sentence corpus to see the whole metric at once. Besides the sentence above, take `U.N. staff met Ekeus in Rome .` (tagged perfectly, 3 true positives) and `Dutch police asked Repsol for data .` where gold is MISC on `Dutch` and ORG on `Repsol`, but the model predicts LOC on `Repsol` and invents ORG on `data`.

Totals over the three sentences: 7 gold entities, 8 predicted, TP 3, FP 5, FN 4.

- precision 3 / 8 = 37.50 percent
- recall 3 / 7 = 42.86 percent
- F1 = 40.00 percent

At the token level the same output is right on 17 of 22 tags, which is 77.3 percent. Two views of one output, 37 points apart.

blocks.prompt: Of the five errors, two are pure boundary slips: the split `San Jose` and the truncated `Mary Smith`. If you fix only those two tags and change nothing else, what happens to precision, recall and F1?
blocks.reveal:
All three jump to 71.43 percent: TP rises from 3 to 5, FP falls from 5 to 2, FN falls from 4 to 2.

Two tags, two fewer false positives *and* two fewer false negatives. A boundary error is charged twice, because the span you emitted is wrong (FP) and the span you were meant to emit is missing (FN). Token accuracy over the same change moves only from 77.3 to 86.4 percent, which is why token accuracy hides the errors that matter most.

blocks.title: Repairing the three-sentence corpus, one error class at a time

scenes.caption: Raw output: TP 3, FP 5, FN 4. Entity F1 is 40.0 percent while token tag accuracy is 77.3 percent.
Fix the two boundary tags only. TP 5, FP 2, FN 2, so all three entity metrics land on 71.43 percent. Token accuracy barely moves, to 86.4 percent.

Also correct the LOC-for-ORG type error and drop the invented entity: TP 6, FP 0, FN 1. Precision is now 100 percent, recall 85.71 percent, F1 92.31 percent. The one remaining miss is the MISC entity.

blocks.md: Never report token accuracy for NER. CoNLL-2003 English training data holds one entity per 8.7 tokens, so the great majority of tags are O and a tagger that predicts O everywhere scores high token accuracy with an entity F1 of exactly zero. Entity-level micro F1 is the metric; token accuracy is a training diagnostic at best.

Two averaging choices are worth keeping straight, because they answer different questions.

**Micro** pools TP, FP and FN across all types, so frequent types dominate. On the toy corpus micro F1 is 40.0 percent.

**Macro** scores each type and averages the per-type F1 values equally. Here LOC gets 33.3, ORG 50.0, PER 50.0 and MISC 0.0 (its single gold entity was missed and nothing MISC was ever predicted), so macro F1 is 33.33 percent. Macro is how you notice that a rare type is dead; micro is what the leaderboard reports. seqeval's `classification_report` prints both, plus the support count per type.

blocks.question: A tagger predicts `B-PER I-PER` over the three tokens `Mary Jane Smith` where gold is one PER spanning all three. What does this contribute to the entity-level counts?
options: 1 TP, since two of three tokens are inside the right entity
1 TP and 1 FP, for getting the type right but the end wrong
0.67 TP under partial credit
1 FP and 1 FN, because the predicted span is not in the gold set and the gold span was not predicted
blocks.explain: Exact match has no partial credit. PER(0,1) is not PER(0,2), so the prediction is a false positive and the gold entity is a false negative. One wrong boundary tag costs two errors, which is why boundary quality drives entity F1 much harder than token accuracy suggests.

blocks.question: Your model scores 91 micro F1 but 68 macro F1 on a five-type corpus. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Micro and macro were computed with different span-matching rules
One or two rare types are performing badly, and micro hides them because frequent types dominate the pooled counts
The model overfits the frequent types, which always lowers micro
Macro is always lower than micro, so the gap means nothing
blocks.explain: Micro pools counts, so the types with most entities set the number. Macro weights every type equally, so one weak rare type drags it down. Reporting both, with per-type support, is how you find the type that needs more data.

lessons.title: Scoring whole sequences: transitions and Viterbi by hand

blocks.md:
A tagger with an independent softmax per token has no idea what it predicted next door. Each position picks its own argmax, so nothing forbids `O` followed by `I-LOC`, and nothing prefers one two-token location over two one-token locations.

This is not a theoretical worry. The Hugging Face token-classification tutorial shows its own fine-tuned model's output on `The Golden State Warriors are an American professional basketball team based in San Francisco.`: it emits `B-location` for `san` and `B-location` again for `francisco`, which the decoder reads as two separate locations, and it splits `Golden State Warriors` into a location followed by a group.

The fix is to score the sequence, not the positions: add a learned score for every label-to-label move, and pick the best-scoring sequence overall.

blocks.title: Independent per-token softmax over three labels

scenes.caption: Token `San`: the encoder is confident this starts a location. Emission scores are 0.2, 2.4 and 0.6; softmax over them gives these percentages.

Token `Francisco`: nearly a coin flip between starting a new location (49.5 percent, scores 1.9) and continuing the current one (40.5 percent, score 1.7). Independent argmax picks B-LOC and splits the entity.
Token `office`: clearly outside, 73.1 percent on O. Three local decisions, and the middle one is where the span breaks.

blocks.md:
A linear-chain conditional random field (CRF) is exactly that extra structure. Lafferty, McCallum and Pereira introduced CRFs in 2001 as undirected models for segmenting and labelling sequences; Huang, Xu and Yu put one on top of a bidirectional LSTM in 2015, and Lample and colleagues made the BiLSTM-CRF the standard NER architecture in 2016.

The model keeps two things. The encoder produces an **emission** matrix $P$, where $P_{i,j}$ scores label $j$ for token $i$. A separate parameter matrix $A$ holds **transition** scores, where $A_{j,k}$ scores moving from label $j$ to label $k$, plus rows for a start and an end state. The score of a whole tag sequence is the sum of both.

blocks.caption: The sequence score from Lample et al. 2016, with y_0 and y_{n+1} the start and end states. Training maximises the log of the softmax of this score over all possible sequences, which is why a CRF is trained on whole sequences rather than per token.

blocks.title: A transition matrix over O, B-LOC, I-LOC

scenes.caption: Illustrative transition scores (learned, not hand-set, in a real model). Positive is encouraged, negative is discouraged.

The one cell that encodes a hard rule: O then I-LOC is invalid under IOB2, and training drives that score strongly negative, here -5.0. No decoded sequence will take it unless the emissions overwhelm it.
The soft preferences matter just as much: continuing a location (B-LOC then I-LOC, +1.5) beats starting a second one (B-LOC then B-LOC, -0.6). That gap is what keeps San Francisco together.

blocks.md:
Now the decoding problem changes. There are $|\mathcal{Y}|^{n}$ possible tag sequences, so you cannot enumerate them: a 20-token sentence with 9 BIO labels has about $1.2 \times 10^{19}$. But the score only couples neighbouring labels, so dynamic programming works. This is the Viterbi algorithm.

Define $\delta_i(j)$ as the best score of any tag prefix that ends at token $i$ with label $j$. Each step extends every prefix by one token and keeps only the best predecessor per label, remembering which one it was (the backpointer).

blocks.caption: One max per label per token: the work is n x |Y| x |Y|, so 20 tokens with 9 labels costs 1,620 edge sums instead of 1.2e19 sequence scores.

blocks.prompt: With the emissions from the bars figure (San: 0.2, 2.4, 0.6; Francisco: 0.3, 1.9, 1.7; office: 2.0, 0.4, 0.2) and the transition matrix above, greedy per-token argmax gives `B-LOC B-LOC O`. What does Viterbi return, and how do the two sequence scores compare?
blocks.reveal:
Viterbi returns `B-LOC I-LOC O` with score 8.4, against 6.4 for the greedy sequence.

Greedy wins the emission at token 2 by 0.2 (1.9 against 1.7) but loses the transition by 2.1 (B-LOC to B-LOC is -0.6, B-LOC to I-LOC is +1.5). Net loss 1.9, plus 0.1 from the following transition into O: 8.4 against 6.4. Under the CRF's own distribution over all 27 sequences, the Viterbi path has probability 0.53 and the greedy path 0.07.

blocks.title: The Viterbi table, filled one token at a time

scenes.caption: Row 1 is the start transition plus the emission. B-LOC gets 0.3 + 2.4 = 2.7, and I-LOC is already dead at -5.0 + 0.6 = -4.4 because a sentence cannot open with I.
Row 2 cell by cell: for I-LOC, max(0.2 - 5.0, 2.7 + 1.5, -4.4 + 1.1) = 4.2, plus emission 1.7, gives 5.9. Every cell in this row has B-LOC as its best predecessor.
Row 3: for O, max(3.4 + 1.2, 4.0 + 0.4, 5.9 + 0.5) = 6.4, plus emission 2.0, gives 8.4. That is the largest value in the last row, so the best sequence ends in O.
Follow the backpointers from 8.4: O came from I-LOC, which came from B-LOC. The decoded path is B-LOC, I-LOC, O, one two-token location. Nine cells of work, not 27 sequences.

blocks.md:
Three things are worth noticing in that table.

First, the invalid transition does its job without any hand-written rule: the illegal sequence `O I-LOC O` scores -0.6 against the winner's 8.4, so it never wins.

Second, the CRF layer earns its keep empirically. Huang and colleagues measured 85.17 F1 for a BiLSTM and 88.83 for the same BiLSTM with a CRF layer on CoNLL-2003 with the pretrained Senna word embeddings. Lample and colleagues report 89.15 for an LSTM tagger and 90.94 for LSTM-CRF, and attribute +1.79 F1 to the CRF layer in their ablation.

Third, do not oversell it. Ratinov and Roth found that in their second-order perceptron tagger, greedy decoding performed comparably to beam search and Viterbi while being over 100 times faster, because entities tend to be short chunks separated by several O tokens, which breaks the sentence into near-independent pieces anyway.

A CRF changes two things at once. At **training** time the loss is over whole sequences, so the model learns which label follows which. At **decoding** time Viterbi returns the best-scoring sequence rather than the best label at each position, so the output is a well-formed tag sequence by construction rather than by repair.

blocks.question: Why is the Viterbi table 3 tokens by 3 labels rather than a list of 27 sequence scores?
options: Because the emissions are independent of each other
Because the transition matrix is symmetric, so half the sequences are duplicates
Because the score only couples adjacent labels, so the best prefix ending in a given label can be reused by every extension of it
Because Viterbi is an approximation that prunes low-scoring sequences
blocks.explain: A linear-chain model has only bigram interactions, so for each label at each position the single best prefix ending there is all you ever need. Viterbi is exact, not an approximation, and that reuse is what turns an exponential count into n x |Y| x |Y| work.

blocks.question: Your BIO tagger has no CRF and sometimes emits `O I-ORG I-ORG`. Which response still leaves that sequence possible?
options: Add a CRF layer so the training loss sees label transitions and Viterbi cannot take an invalid one
Switch to BIOES so the output layer has 17 labels instead of 9
Keep the independent softmax but mask out transitions the scheme forbids during decoding
Decode with a beam that only extends well-formed BIO prefixes
blocks.explain: BIOES makes the tag set larger and the end of a span explicit, but with independent per-token softmaxes nothing rules out an impossible sequence: you can still emit O then I-ORG, now with 17 labels. The other three all make the invalid path unreachable, either in the loss or in the decoder.

blocks.md:
A transformer tagger is the same recipe with a better encoder. Run the sentence through the model, take each token's final hidden state, and apply one shared linear layer to get $|\mathcal{Y}|$ scores per token.

The BERT paper did exactly this on CoNLL-2003: a case-preserving WordPiece input with the maximal document context the data provides, formulated as a tagging task with, in their words, no CRF layer. Fine-tuned BERT-large scored 96.6 dev and 92.8 test F1; BERT-base scored 96.4 and 92.4. For comparison, the best 2003 system scored 88.76 test F1 with hand-built features and gazetteers.

There is a catch that the earlier architectures did not have. Your labels are per word, but the model's inputs are subword pieces, and the two do not line up.

The BERT paper's answer is one line: "We use the representation of the first sub-token as the input to the token-level classifier over the NER label set."

In code, the tokenizer tells you which word each piece came from. The Hugging Face [token classification guide](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/tasks/token_classification) does the bookkeeping with three rules:

1. map every piece to its word with `word_ids()`,
2. give the special tokens the label -100, which PyTorch's cross-entropy ignores,
3. label only the first piece of each word, and give the continuation pieces -100 too.

The guide's own example makes the mismatch concrete: the WNUT 17 word `ESB`, labelled `B-location`, becomes the two pieces `es` and `##b`.

blocks.title: Aligning word labels to WordPiece tokens

scenes.caption: Three words (`=`, `ESB`, `.`) become four pieces plus two special tokens. word_ids() reports None for the specials and 1 twice for ESB.
The word labels are O, B-LOC, O. Only the first piece of each word keeps its label; specials and continuation pieces get -100, so the loss ignores them.

At inference the tag predicted for the first piece becomes the word's tag and the rest are dropped, so the span decoder and the metric both run on the 3 words. Scoring the 6 pieces instead would compare against a different gold sequence.

blocks.title: The alignment loop, one piece at a time

scenes.caption: Three word tags go in, six piece labels come out.
[CLS] has no word, so it gets -100 and contributes nothing to the loss.
Word 0 is new, so its piece takes the word's tag O.
Word 1 is new at piece `es`, which therefore carries B-LOC. This is the sub-token the classifier is trained on.
The second piece of word 1, `##b`, repeats the word id, so it is masked out with -100. Labelling it I-LOC instead would teach the model to open spans mid-word.
The remaining word and the final special token finish the sequence: 6 labels, of which 3 are real.

blocks.md:
Two alignment bugs cost real F1 and neither one crashes.

Labelling continuation pieces with `I-X` instead of -100 teaches the model that spans can start and continue inside a word, which leaks into the decoder.

Evaluating on pieces instead of words changes the number of gold entities, so your F1 is not comparable to anyone else's. Map back to words first, then score.

Does a transformer still need a CRF on top? The evidence in this course says the CRF gains were measured on BiLSTM encoders (Huang: 85.17 to 88.83; Lample: +1.79 F1), and that BERT reached 92.8 test F1 with a plain softmax and no CRF. A strong encoder already sees the whole sentence through self-attention, so much of what the transition matrix provided is available in the emissions.

What a CRF still gives you is a guarantee about the *shape* of the output. If downstream code assumes well-formed BIOES spans, a CRF or a constrained Viterbi decoder is a cheap way to make that true by construction instead of patching tag sequences after the fact.

blocks.question: You fine-tune a BERT tagger and score 94 F1 on your own eval but 89 when a colleague scores the same predictions. The only difference is that you evaluated on WordPiece tokens and they evaluated on words. Why can your number be higher?
options: WordPiece tokens are easier to classify than words
You scored a different gold sequence, since masked continuation pieces and specials change the entity set and the counts
Scoring on pieces double counts true positives but not false positives
The discrepancy means the alignment code is broken
blocks.explain: The metric counts spans over whatever unit you give it. Pieces and words are different sequences with different entity boundaries, so the two runs are measuring different problems. Only the word-level number is comparable to published results.

blocks.question: In the Hugging Face recipe, why do continuation sub-pieces get -100 rather than the word's label?
options: Because -100 is a reserved label id for the O class
Because the loss would otherwise be dominated by long words
Because the tokenizer cannot tell which word a continuation piece belongs to
Because the classifier is trained and read out on the first piece of each word, so the other pieces must be excluded from the loss
blocks.explain: -100 is the ignore index of PyTorch's cross-entropy, not a class. The convention is one prediction per word, taken at the word's first piece, exactly as the BERT paper describes, so every other piece must be masked out of the loss.

lessons.title: Few labels, new domain, and the failure modes that remain

blocks.md:
Now take a tagger trained on CoNLL-2003 and point it at your logs. It will do badly, for reasons that have nothing to do with model quality.

The **label set is wrong**. You want HOST, COMPONENT and ERROR_CODE; the model knows PER, LOC, ORG and MISC. There is no mapping, so even a perfect newswire tagger scores zero on your task.

The **features are wrong**. Most of the sixteen CoNLL-2003 entries used orthographic features (12 of 16, by the paper's own feature table), because a capitalised word in newswire is a strong entity signal. In `web-04 ERROR authd code=E503 db-7 timed out` capitalisation marks the severity, not the entities.

And you have almost no labels. Hand-annotating 15,000 sentences is how CoNLL-2003 was built; you have an afternoon. The practical route is **weak supervision**: write programs that label data, then train on their output.

blocks.title: A weak-supervision pipeline for log entities

scenes.caption: Start from unlabelled logs and three labelling functions: a regex for host names, a gazetteer exported from the configuration management database, and a regex for error codes. Each is cheap, narrow and wrong sometimes.

Each function votes on each token, abstaining where it does not match. An aggregator estimates how accurate each one is and resolves the disagreements; this is what the skweak toolkit does with a generative model.
The aggregated votes become a large, noisy training set. A tagger trained on it generalises past the regexes, because it also sees the context around each match.
A small hand-labelled set does two jobs that weak supervision cannot: it fine-tunes the tagger at the end, and it is the only honest measurement of entity F1.

blocks.md:
Run those three labelling functions over one tokenised line and watch what you get. The line is `web-04 ERROR authd code = E503 db-7 timed out` (9 tokens) and the gold entities are HOST on `web-04`, COMPONENT on `authd`, ERROR_CODE on `E503` and HOST on `db-7`.

- the host regex `[a-z]+-[0-9]+` fires on 2 of 9 tokens (22 percent coverage): `web-04`, `db-7`
- the CMDB gazetteer fires on 2 of 9 (22 percent): `authd`, `db-7`
- the error-code regex `E[0-9]{3}` fires on 1 of 9 (11 percent): `E503`

Each function abstains on most tokens, which is normal: coverage comes from having many of them. One token, `db-7`, gets two different labels, and how you break that tie decides your score.

blocks.title: Three labelling functions voting on one log line

scenes.caption: The tokenised line. In production these lines are unlabelled; the 4 gold entities are known here only so the merge can be scored in the last scene.
The host regex matches a lowercase word followed by a digit group: 2 of 9 tokens.
The CMDB gazetteer adds `authd`, which the regex missed entirely, and also claims `db-7`. Two functions now disagree about one token.
The error-code regex covers the one token neither of the others touches.

Merging code first, then host, then gazetteer recovers all 4 gold entities: 100 percent precision and recall here. Preferring the gazetteer on `db-7` gives TP 3, FP 1, FN 1, or 75 percent. Simplified: one 9-token line.

blocks.title: The tie-break on one token moves every metric

scenes.caption: Gazetteer wins `db-7`: TP 3, FP 1, FN 1 against the 4 gold entities, so 75 percent across the board.
Host regex wins `db-7`: TP 4, FP 0, FN 0. Nine tokens, so treat this as a demonstration of sensitivity, not as a measured result.

blocks.md:
That is why aggregation is a model and not an if-statement. The [skweak](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09683) toolkit lets you write labelling functions (heuristics, gazetteers, regexes, even other models) and then aggregate them with a generative model that estimates each function's accuracy and confusions from their agreement pattern alone, with no gold labels. You keep the small hand-labelled set for fine-tuning and for evaluation, which is the one thing weak supervision cannot replace.

The practical order of work: label a few hundred lines by hand first, so you can measure anything at all; write labelling functions until coverage is decent; train a tagger on the aggregated output; fine-tune on the gold set; then iterate on the labelling functions by reading the errors.

Three failure modes survive all of this, and it is better to know them than to be surprised.

**Nested entities.** A linear chain assigns one label per token, so it cannot say that `Bank of China` is an organisation containing the location `China`. CoNLL-2003 sidesteps this by annotating only the top-level entity, but the nesting is really there: Finkel and Manning report that roughly 17 percent of entities in the GENIA biomedical corpus are embedded in another entity, and nearly half in the AnCora corpus. If your entities nest, you need a different output structure, not a better chain.

**Boundary errors.** The most common residual error, and the most expensive: one wrong edge costs a false positive and a false negative, as you computed in lesson 3.

**Label noise.** Your gold set is not gold. CrossWeigh found that about 5.38 percent of CoNLL-2003 test sentences contain label mistakes, sixteen years after publication. On a hastily annotated internal set, expect worse, and expect a few points of your F1 to be annotation disagreement rather than model error.

When labels are scarce, spend them on **measurement** first and **training** second. A few hundred carefully labelled lines plus a pile of noisily labelled ones beats a thousand rushed labels with no held-out set, because without a trustworthy eval you cannot tell whether any change helped.

blocks.question: Your log tagger scores 91 F1 on a weakly labelled held-out split and 62 F1 on 200 hand-labelled lines. What is the most likely cause?
options: The weakly labelled split shares the labelling functions' blind spots, so it rewards reproducing them rather than finding entities
The hand-labelled set is too small for the metric to be meaningful
The model overfitted the 200 hand-labelled lines
Entity F1 is not comparable across splits
blocks.explain: A test set built by the same regexes and gazetteers as the training labels cannot reveal what those functions miss. The tagger gets credit for imitating them. Only human labels measure the task, which is why some of your annotation budget must be held out and never used for training.

blocks.question: Which of these is a structural limitation of BIO tagging that no amount of training data fixes?
options: It cannot represent single-token entities
It cannot represent entities of more than one type in a sentence
It cannot represent an entity nested inside another entity
It cannot represent adjacent entities of the same type
blocks.explain: BIO handles single-token entities (B alone), many types per sentence, and adjacency (that is what B is for). What one label per token cannot encode is overlap: a token inside both an ORG and a LOC needs two labels, which is why nested NER uses hypergraphs, spans or parse structures instead.
